lines.text: A small desert peninsula of pearl divers that became one of the richest countries on Earth. This is the story of Qatar.
On the north-west coast, Al Zubarah grew into a busy town of pearl divers and traders. Its ruins are now a World Heritage site.
In the early nineteenth century, the Al Thani family rose to lead Qatar, and they have ruled it ever since.
A fishing village on the east coast, Doha, became their seat. One day it would be a city of towers.
Around 1870, Qatar emerged as a land of its own under the Al Thani.
In 1938 a fort was built beside the old ruins of Al Zubarah, where it still stands.
Hamad bin Khalifa was born in 1952. As emir, he would make Qatar rich and known around the world.
In 1971, the year of independence, the North Field was found offshore, the largest natural gas field in the world.
Tamim bin Hamad, born in 1980, would succeed his father and become emir in 2013.
Mutaz Essa Barshim, born in 1991, would share the Olympic high jump gold in Tokyo.
In 1993 Qatar Airways was founded, the national airline.
The Qatar Foundation built Education City, bringing branches of foreign universities to Doha.
In 1996 Al Jazeera began broadcasting from Doha, giving Arab viewers an independent news channel, and later one in English.
In 2006 Doha hosted the Asian Games, the first great sports event in the Gulf.
Two years later, I. M. Pei's Museum of Islamic Art opened on the waterfront.
In 2017 Saudi Arabia and its allies cut ties and imposed a blockade. It lasted until 2021.
In 2019 the National Museum of Qatar opened, designed by Jean Nouvel in the shape of a desert rose.
In 2022 Qatar hosted the first World Cup in the Middle East. Argentina and Messi beat France on penalties in a final for the ages.
That final was played at Lusail Stadium, the crowning moment of Qatar's rise.
From pearls to gas and global sport, Qatar travelled a long way in a short time.
